To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the incidence of hypersensitivity reactions was 4.4% and that skin tests with platinum salts and pementrexed were not predictive of hypersensitivity reactions.
the most common hypersensitivity reactions were urticaria and angioedema.

(i) hypersensitivity reactions to chemotherapy are not rare in thoracic oncology; (ii) the most frequently encountered reactions are related to platinum‐based chemotherapy; (iii) the most common symptoms were cutaneous and gastrointestinal; (iv) the most frequent reactions were grade I and II; (v) the most common grade III reactions were anaphylaxis and angioedema and (vi) skin tests to platinum salts were negative in most patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of hypersensitivity reaction (HSR) induced by chemotherapeutics in patients with thoracic malignancies, and the value of skin testing for platinum salts and Pemetrexed in predicting the occurrence of HSR.
the development and application of novel methods and tools in the field of chemical reaction engineering.
the study of hypersensitivity and allergy to chemotherapeutic drugs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hypersensitivity reactions to chemotherapy drugs can be managed by a combination of desensitization and skin tests.

there is no conclusive evidence that skin testing to platinum salts is of value for predicting hypersensitivity reactions to carboplatin or oxaliplatin, and that skin testing to pemetrexed is not of value in predicting hypersensitivity reactions in patients with non‐smal cell lung cancer or malignant pleural.

the evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the routine use of skin tests to predict or prevent hypersensitivity reactions to platinum‐based chemotherapy in patients with non‐surgical cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hypersensitivity reactions are a frequent and unpredictable event in patients with thoracic malignancies receiving platinum salts or pemetrexed.
hypersensitivity reactions to chemotherapy in patients with thoracic malignancy are common, but can be prevented or treated with desensitization protocols.

the hypersensitivity reactions to platinum salts and pematrexed in patients with non‐smal cell lung cancer and malignant pleural mesotheioma are common, and that skin tests can be useful in the diagnosis and treatment of hypersensitivity reactions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hypersensitivity reactions to platinum salts and pematrexed can be predicted using skin testing.
the use of pemetrexed is associated with a lower incidence of hypersensitivity reactions.
skin testing for platinum salts is not helpful for the prevention of hypersensitivity reactions in patients who are receiving pemetrexed‐containing regimens.
